implementation_notes: Every Scala reference is an AnyRef with a JVM monitor, so `lock.synchronized { body }` is the native scope-bound form: the compiler emits monitorenter/monitorexit with an implicit handler and exceptions release the monitor. For explicit locks, java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock is fully usable but has no stdlib withLock wrapper, so the guard is a try/finally around lock()/unlock() - the one Scala case where the pattern must be hand-written. For state that can be replaced rather than mutated, atomic references (AtomicReference.updateAndGet/compareAndSet) and immutable collections remove the need for a scope entirely.
pitfalls: `synchronized` on `this` (the implicit target of synchronized methods) lets outside code lock the same monitor; lock on a dedicated private object.
By-name bodies and closures can outlive the block: returning a lazy value or scheduling a Future inside synchronized runs the real work after the monitor is released.

The try/finally form around ReentrantLock has the same missing-unlock risk as Java and no compiler check; never return from the try before the finally runs (it always runs, but state may be half-updated).
Blocking on a monitor inside a Future/ExecutionContext callback can starve the pool; use non-blocking atomic updates or a dedicated execution context.
